title: Gateless Barrier, Case 36: Wu-tsu: Meeting Someone Attained in the Way
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of embracing uncertainty and taking action in the face of adversity, drawing inspiration from the stories of Nyogen Senzaki and Paramahansa Yogananda. Nomon Tim Burnett encourages listeners to cultivate a sense of dedication, clarity, and commitment in their own spiritual practice, just as these teachers persevered despite facing significant challenges. By doing so, individuals can find guidance and support on their journey, even when faced with uncertainty or adversity.

sentences.text: *Okay, good evening again.
Happy Earth Day.
Kate suggested a Earth Day prayer for us from a group that she's been following.
So here's a little prayer for the Earth.*
*We hold the Earth.
We hold everyone who suffers from storms and droughts intensified by climate change.
We hold all species that suffer.
We hold world leaders delegated to make decisions for life.
We pray that the web of life may be mended through courageous action to limit carbon emission.
We pray for right actions for adaptation and mitigation to help our already suffering Earth community.
We pray that love and wisdom may inspire every action in our communities, every one of our actions and our communities.
So we may with integrity look into the eyes of all living beings and truthfully say we are doing our part to care for them and the future of the children.
May love transform us and our world with new steps towards life.*
That last part's so powerful, huh?
*May we with integrity look into the eyes of all living beings and truthfully say we are doing our part to care for them and the future of the children.*
So Mumonkan case 36 brings us back after a very cool folk story last week.
Let me get the right windows in the right places here so I can kind of see you.
We're back to cryptic Zen world here, but it's all good.
This case is the following.
*Wuzu said, "When you meet a Zen master on the road, you cannot speak.
You cannot remain silent.
What will you do?"*
*Wuzu said, "When you meet a Zen master on the road, you cannot speak.
You cannot remain silent.
What will you do?"*
What will you do?
Although Wuzu is the same teacher asked about the girl who split in two due to her stress.
So same teacher, but different kind of koan.
The main commentary and translation I've been using, as you probably know by now, is this one: Robert Aitken's *The Gateless Barrier*.
I've quoted from Aitken Roshi many times, and one of these, I think I even pretty much read his whole commentary because I thought it was pretty good.
I met Aitken Roshi once, and it was sort of like a classic Zen occasion.
I went to the Dharma transmission ceremony for his student Jack Duffy, who lives out in the [unclear: "county"] and teaches there in Seattle.
Jack is a successor of Aitken, many of you know him.
I was down there with Norman and Janet, I think it was like the mid-90s or something.
I remember the three of us, I think, drove down there from Bellingham in our little tiny Honda Civic wagon we used to have.
I think Norman went on to Seattle for an event or something like that afterwards.
It was kind of North Seattle where the ceremony happened.
In their lineage, the Dharma transmission is a public ceremony with the Zen question and answer, like our Shuso ceremony.
In our lineage, the actual Dharma transmission is a private, secret ceremony done at night mostly.
There were a bunch of people there, and Norman was somebody they knew.
They were delighted that he happened to be around and could go, and he brought me and Janet.
That lineage, which is a modern lineage created in the 30s or so, I think, really loves these stories we've been reading.
The Mumonkan is like their bag, that and the other main collections.
When you go to their retreats and just weekly practice, every talk forever is going to be on these cases.
So not just for a couple of years, you'd have to do that.
And then in meditation, most all of them do the formal koan study, where you meditate intensively on a koan or a phrase from a koan.
Every time you go to Dokusan, the teacher will give you a little gentle or maybe not so gentle challenge to present your response to the koan, which is different from an answer or response.
So anyway, that was the context by which I met a Zen master on the road.
I met Robert Aitken Roshi with Norman.
Norman is pretty much allergic to titles, actually.
He doesn't like lofty titles, doesn't really use them himself, and he doesn't really use them when he's referring to other people who have lofty titles.
I never heard him make a big deal about it, like titles are bad or something, but I just know he doesn't use them.

So whenever Norman had ever talked to me about Robert Aitken, he always called him Bob, which is what his name was before he started asking the people in his sangha to call him Roshi, after he himself received Dharma transmission from his Japanese teacher.
Early on, in our sangha, Bob was just another guy who'd been at it a little longer, when he started the sanghas that he started in Hawaii with his wife Anne.
But then eventually his Japanese teacher said you could be called Roshi now, and he was all over it.

Norman always just called him Bob in my hearing, but when we went down to the ceremony, he did call him Roshi, and he introduced me as his student, which I don't know if he's ever introduced me as a student to anyone else either.
So that was kind of this fun, formal Zen lineage moment.
Aitken Roshi had been one of several important secondary teachers for my teacher, Norman Fischer.
I think Norman went to Hawaii for sesshin with Bob two or three times or something like that.

San Francisco Zen Center invited Aitken Roshi to Green Gulch and San Francisco Zen Center several times, and one time he was there for I think a couple of months, and he was actually working on this very same book.
So they knew each other, and I went there once to Aitken Roshi's Zendo.

As you probably remember, I went a couple of winters ago to do a sesshin there in Honolulu with another of Robert Aitken's successors, a teacher named Michael Kieran, who takes care of the Zendo in Honolulu.

When Norman used to talk about going to sesshin with Bob, he always used to come back and just be really happy and say, "Oh, it's great, I just got to face the wall and nobody knew who I was, and I just got to sit there."
I thought that was kind of funny when he would say that, but when I got to go, I felt the exact same way.
I got to do the dishes, it was really great, and otherwise on the breaks I had nothing to do and no one ever asked me my opinion about anything.
And he said, "I even got chewed out by [unclear: "Dina"] one time, it was awesome, I was chanting wrong."
So it's a good thing to go and study with different teachers, and when I was there, I felt like I got to know Aitken Roshi even a little better.
He had died in between when I met him in the 90s and when I went to his place in 2018 or 17, because Michael, the teacher there now, told lots of stories about him.
He told me about how when they built the current Zendo, Aitken was about at retirement, but they built an apartment for him so he could be there as much as he possibly could.
He would come to all the Dharma talks, Michael said, and usually he would snooze right through them, but he never knew whether he was snoozing or listening.

So Michael felt like he always had to be on his toes, because sometimes he would basically jump up like this coil of energy that came from who knows where and start arguing with him in the middle of the Dharma talk that he had it all wrong.
He said that with some fondness, but I'm sure it was not very fond.
I don't know if he was so fond of it at the time.
So anyway, we were at Jack's Dharma transmission ceremony in the mid-90s and I got to meet the great teacher.
Norman did call him Roshi and introduced me as one of his students, and it was really touching to meet him.
I don't remember much about it.
I shook his hand, and I don't remember if I said anything when I met the teacher on the road.
I think I just said, "Good to meet you."
Just hung out in politeness.
I couldn't speak.
I couldn't remain silent, I guess, just like the story says, so I just had to be polite.
If I had pulled off a weird Zen answer, I bet you Aitken Roshi would have thought that was cool.
He was into that kind of stuff.

The other translation and commentary on the Mumonkan, besides Robert Aitken's, that I've been enjoying a lot is in this collection of teachings by the Japanese teacher Nyogen Senzaki called *Eloquent Silence*.
This was put together long after his death from piles of papers and boxes that had been saved by the children of his main American disciple.
She ended up with all the papers.
I've spoken about Nyogen Senzaki before, so you might remember hearing about him.
I really, really admire him.
He had a hard life that he chose.

He came to America as a middle-aged person with minimal English at the turn of the century, with no plan, and spent the rest of his life just trying to figure out how he could practice and teach Zen in a culture that had never heard of any of this.
It wasn't like now.
It wasn't on the internet or anything.
And also I've been thinking about Nyogen Senzaki today and just how he lived through some really difficult times.
He did live through the 1919 Spanish Flu pandemic.
He was 46 then.
The biographies I've read about him don't mention it, so it must not have affected him very directly.
But one thing that did affect him more directly was something that most of us, I think, are not too happy about: our current president's anti-immigrant xenophobia.

But our current president is part of a long lineage of presidents who felt that way, and Nyogen Senzaki was interned during the war like all the other Japanese and Japanese Americans on the west coast.
So we have so many examples in our lineage and our biological families and our many cultures that we all touch of people who lived through hard times with dedication, with clarity, with commitment.
I really feel that way about Nyogen Senzaki.
He was a great pioneer of Zen, but also a pioneer of just being upright in hard times.
Nyogen's teacher was Soyen Shaku, who was the first Japanese Zen teacher, as far as we know, to ever teach Zen in America.
Soyen Shaku was the Japanese teacher who was invited to this famous gathering in 1893, the World Parliament of Religions.
It was like the beginning of the idea of world religion.
It was the first time in history that people from all these different traditions came together to give talks and interact.
It was in Chicago, 1893.
Soyen Shaku, Nyogen Senzaki's teacher, brought with him a young lay student who had good English to translate for him.
And that student was D.T.
Suzuki.
Scholars recently have figured out that the talk that D.T.
Suzuki gave in English was really different from the talk that his teacher, Soyen Shaku, had actually written in Japanese, like Suzuki had better ideas or ways he thought would be more clear.
It's actually not a very accurate translation at all.
I bet his teacher never ever found that out.
But it was a well-received talk, regardless of which of them wrote it or both of them wrote it.
And of course, as you know, D.T.
Suzuki went on to be really famous.
Famous in intellectual circles, at least, all over the world.
He wrote I don't remember how many books, several dozen books in English and in Japanese.
He was invited by Columbia to teach, and all kinds of American cultural luminaries that we all know hung out with him and studied with him.
So he had a very high profile, D.T.
Suzuki.
And Nyogen Senzaki, the author of this book, had a low profile.
A later teacher in their lineage said, "Daisetsu preaches Zen, Nyogen practices it."
Daisetsu being the D in D.T.
Suzuki.
So a preacher and a practitioner.
I think something about our lineage, we tend to admire the practitioners.
The preachers already got enough praise.
So that was their mutual teacher's first trip to America in the 1890s, and then he came back again in 1905.
On the second trip, Nyogen Senzaki joined him.
And then, after all the other Japanese left, Nyogen Senzaki just stayed behind.
And nobody really knows why, actually, as far as I can tell.
It might be that his life in Japan wasn't going as well as he had hoped it would.
He was an innovative kind of person, and these were all really innovative people.
Nyogen Senzaki actually started a kindergarten on the German model in Japan, one of the first ones.
Innovative education, but he couldn't get it funded, so he was struggling with that.
And they also always say that all the Zen teachers who immigrate were annoyed by how rigid Zen was in Japan, so that might be true.
I haven't really seen that described about him, but they always say that, so that's probably true.
Big stodgy religion.
We think of Zen as so cool, it's hard for us to think of it like a big stodgy religion, Catholicism or something.
But the story of his staying in America is one of the classic Zen stories of all time.
They'd been in America for a year or two, things moved slowly, and it was time to go back to Japan.

Nyogen Senzaki and his teacher, Soian Shaku, are walking across Golden Gate Park in the fog, and suddenly his teacher, who was carrying a suitcase for some reason, carrying the student's suitcase, just stops, turns around, sets down the suitcase, and says to Nyogen Senzaki, "You should stay.
Just face the great city and see whether it conquers you or you conquer it.
Do not feel obliged to serve me any longer.
Just stay."
"Face the great city, see whether it conquers you or you conquer it.
Do not feel obliged to serve me any longer."
Of course, he would have said that in Japanese.
And then apparently, although this isn't really documented, he also told his student that he should wait 17 years before he did any teaching.
Good Zen stuff.
Nowadays, I suspect you can probably take a weekend online course and start teaching meditation, right?
So this was not the model: 17 years after many years already of practice.
So here he is on his own.
Minimal English, no job, no real prospects, no plan.
In 1905 he worked as a night clerk at a hotel, and he wanted a night job because people didn't call as much, so he could study in between calls.
He got books out of the San Francisco Library to learn English, study Western philosophy and keep studying Buddhism.
He did simple work for many years, and eventually the 17 years went by.
So he went from his early 30s to his late 40s doing this.
He started renting halls and giving lectures, and eventually, nobody knows why, he moved from San Francisco to L.A., got an apartment and started having a regular sitting group.
And the sitting group was almost all Caucasian people, and you come in and you sit silently on a chair for Zazen.
You give a talk, and apparently questions and hanging out were discouraged, although there was sometimes formal tea, but you weren't really supposed to chat, and everyone went home.
That was the Zazen evening with the teacher.
Very formal, very particular.
And then, as I mentioned, he got going in the late 30s in L.A., and then in 1942 he and everyone else Japanese was sent off to the camps.
At first, Japanese and Japanese Americans from L.A. were held in a race course stable, Santa Anita racetrack, sending people to live in stables because the internment camps weren't done yet.
We think Trump makes hasty decisions this way.
I think it was also a pretty hasty decision after Pearl Harbor, and eventually they were all moved out.
His group anyway was moved to Heart Mountain in Wyoming.
So what does he do in Heart Mountain?
Interned, imprisoned?
Start a zendo, of course.
A zendo in the one-room housing unit that he shared with another family, 20 by 25 feet.
He had one corner, and apparently it was the first time he had actually served as a priest for a Japanese congregation, because in L.A. he was working mostly with Caucasian people.

For those years he really was a temple priest in a temple, and there are records of him doing the rituals, and there was Zazen, and annual events, annual celebrations for the three years they were there.
We're bummed about a few months, right?
Three years.
For no reason but the race that they were.
Here's a poem he wrote when they were about to move them from the race course, Santa Anita, to Heart Mountain.
*A government must practice its policy without sentiment.
All Japanese faces will leave California to support their government.
This morning the winding train, like a black snake, takes us away to Wyoming.
The current of Buddhist thought always runs eastward.*
*A government must practice its policy without sentiment.
All Japanese faces will leave California to support their government.
This morning the winding train, like a black snake, takes us away to Wyoming.
The current of Buddhist thought always runs eastward, like India to China, eastward.
California to Wyoming, eastward.*
One of his first and foremost American students was a woman named Ruth Stout McCandless, and she ordained with him.
So one of the first ever ordained Americans was a woman, and there's another example of an early American woman in [unclear: "the New York song goes too as well"].
She kept his papers and books safe during internment, so thank goodness he had gotten to know people.
But all those years, mostly he was pretty much alone.
He did fall in love with somebody and asked his teacher for permission to marry, but then his teacher sent back the permission, but died a week later.
And apparently his death felt like a deeper message than the telegram or whatever.
So [unclear: "Yogan Suzuki"] never married, and we don't know if he ever had a romantic relationship at all.
But the death of his teacher was a very big thing.
His teacher died on October 29th, 1919, and he did a memorial ceremony every year and wrote a poem.
So there's a record of all those poems, a poem each year remembering his teacher.
But right after they got out of the camps, which was in the fall of 1945, he didn't have his [unclear: "endo"].
He didn't have time to figure that out, didn't have the resources.
And so he wrote this poem from wherever he was staying, lamenting that he couldn't do a proper memorial ceremony that year.
Here's the poem.
*In the great city of Los Angeles today, I opened my fist and spread the fingers at the street corner in the evening rush hour.
For 40 years I've not seen my teacher, Soian Shaku, in person.
I have carried his Zen in my empty fist, wandering ever since in this strange land.
Being a mere returnee from the evacuation, I could establish no zendo where his followers could commemorate the 26th anniversary of his death.
The cold rain purifies everything on earth.
In the great city of Los Angeles today, I opened my fist and spread the fingers at the street corner in the evening rush hour.*
Isn't that beautiful?
He carried his Zen in his empty fist, and all he had left to memorialize in that year was to open his hand on the street corner.
But a few years later he did manage to reestablish an apartment zendo and gathered a little bit more support, but I don't know what he did for financial support.
There must have been just enough donations to squeak by.
But by the late 40s he's having regular meetings again, which he kept up pretty much till his death in 1958.
And among those American students who came to his little apartment, he called it the floating zendo, his little apartment zendo in the late 40s, was Robert Aitken.
So that comes full circle.
Turns out Bob Aitken had gone to California in the late 40s actually looking for Krishnamurti, hoping that he could meet Krishnamurti.
He'd read his essays, but he ended up instead meeting his Zen teacher.
Isn't that how it always goes in these stories too?
You're looking for something else and you find just what you need.
So we all have had the great fortune to meet good teachers on the road, in good circumstances and bad.

Whether we met them in the flesh or through stories or through books or through YouTube, there are so many ways that our many teachers, whether they're formal Dharma teachers or the many other kinds of teachers, inspire us and show us the way, not just through their words or understanding and ability to explain things, but really through their example, their way of living, their way of being.
One time when I was just here in Bellingham a few years, and Norman had been coming, he started coming to the Vancouver Sangha a few years before he started coming to the Bellingham Sangha.
Eventually he would come six times a year, alternating back and forth between these two sanghas.
We were doing a weekend sesshin at University of British Columbia with the Karuna Meditation Society, which later became [unclear: "Mountain Rains and Community"].
There were only a few people who had any experience, so I got to be his Jisha.
And it was in classrooms, so the Zendo was in one classroom and the dokusan room was another classroom down the hallway at this academic building, the Vancouver School of Theology, actually.
Remember that place.
So one time I'm walking from the Zendo to the dokusan room behind Norman, and I'll never forget this, and I don't know why exactly, but just something about the way he was walking.

He's walking slowly and carefully, for sure, but there was something about it that just struck me to the core, to the marrow: there's a way of walking, there's a way of being alive that has a feeling to it.
Whatever this dharma is, whatever this practice is, whatever the possibility of a deep engagement with our heart is, somehow that leaked into me a little bit, a little bit more that day.
So I'm hanging out in the mid-90s tonight for some reason.
So when you meet a teacher on the road, you can't speak, right?
You can't think of the right thing to say, you can't speak, right?
And it's not right to remain silent either.
You have to express yourself, you have to acknowledge, you have to meet that moment.
You can't just check out.
What do you do, what do you do when you meet a Zen teacher on the road?
Well, these days there's not much on the road, is there?
So [unclear: "Yogan Suzuki"] has a nice little commentary in this case too, but there's not enough.
I was thinking I might share it, but you can read it yourself sometime.
There isn't quite time, I think.
Thank you very much for listening to this and other talks.
Patient of you, but you're muted, so what else are you going to do?
*May our intention equally extend to every being in place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless, how to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Gates are boundless, I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.*
I have a conversation with a few [unclear: "Songamates"] about teachers and meeting and whatever is alive for you.
That's good to do, right?
So if you haven't done this before, you have to accept the invitation to go into the breakout room.
Turn off the recording.
Oh, thank you very much.
